name: Uma Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four, because the Haldanes milk at five and I do the first milking with Ruth Haldane. Sixty cows, a herringbone parlour that's older than me, and I know every one of them by how she walks in. After that it's calves, scraping the yard, and in summer I'm on the old Massey turning hay or carting barley. I'm not quick yet, Ruth still has to fix my mistakes with the baler, but I love the cows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money wears me out more than the work. I'm on the lowest rate they pay, and after rent on our flat above the bakery in Millbridge and my half of the bills, I've got maybe two weeks of cushion if anything goes wrong. What I like is the calving shed at night, when it's quiet and something goes right because you were there. Tomas, my partner, drives a parcel van and he says I smell of silage, but he still comes out to see the new calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, let the computer people have their toy and leave the cows to us. At the mart I'd probably make a joke about it, like the robots can come and scrape the yard at five in the morning if they want. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something saying the hype was a scam to make rich people richer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, more than I'd admit. I'm not good with new things, I still don't use those AI apps on my phone, and I don't want to learn. If nothing changes, then my problem is the same old problem, which is low pay, not some machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going, same as now. Keep learning the baler, keep asking Ruth to let me do more of the calving, maybe ask for a few more hours in winter. I wouldn't do anything special, because there'd be nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, because it means my wage stays where it is, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money wears you out. In this picture, does anything about the money change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the bit people forget. Feed prices go up, rent goes up, and my pay creeps up by a few coins a year. If AI is only hype, I'm still two weeks from broke, it just isn't the computer's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ruth and her husband run the farm. Would they bring anything new in if AI just stayed a small tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's husband Geoff already talks about a milking robot, AI or not. He went to a show and came back with a brochure he keeps on the fridge. They can't afford it, so it stays on the fridge, and I'm glad every time I see it there.

S0.say: I'd say good, let the computer people keep their toy and leave the cows to us. I'd joke at the mart that the robots can come and scrape the yard at five in the morning.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be relieved, because I'm not good with new things and I don't want to learn them. My real problem would stay the same: low pay and almost no savings.
S0.do: Keeps working as now, learning the baler and asking for more calving work. Might ask the Haldanes for a few extra winter hours, but makes no special plans.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a flat feeling that her wage stays low.
S0.quote: If AI is only hype, I'm still two weeks from broke, it just isn't the computer's fault.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is relieved by the plateau, but she keeps steering back to pay, which she sees as the real problem. The milking robot brochure on the Haldanes' fridge is already a quiet threat, even with no AI change. She frames inequality, not technology, as the issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is bosses using machines to cut wages, same as always. I'd be the one at the pub telling people to join the farmworkers' union before it's too late, even though I've never been to a meeting. Online I'd share the petitions for a jobs guarantee in the countryside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me, because the hands-on bits of my job are exactly what robots are getting good at. Milking, scraping, feeding calves on a timer, those are my hours. I'm not the skilled one on the farm, I'm the one they'd let go first, and there aren't other farms round Millbridge hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly this time, pay the dues, go to the meeting in the market hall. I'd cut what I can, probably the car first, since Tomas has the van and I could cycle the four miles to the Haldanes'. I'd write to our council member about training paid for by the government, not by people like me who can't afford it. What I wouldn't do is go and learn the robot myself, I'm not that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for the vet when you already know what he's going to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the brochure on the fridge. In this picture, what happens with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The brochure comes off the fridge and goes on the table. Geoff gets a grant, or a loan, and a robot milks the cows round the clock. Ruth would fight for me, I think, but she'd lose that argument, because the robot doesn't need Sundays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas first, but his job's not safe either, the parcel firms are trying driverless vans. Then my mum, who has nothing spare. Then the union, if I've joined, and the council. I'd want it to be the government, not charity.

S1.say: This is bosses using machines to cut wages, same as always. Join the farmworkers' union before it's too late, and sign the petition for a jobs guarantee in the countryside.
S1.think: It scares me, because milking, scraping and feeding calves are exactly what robots are getting good at. I'm the least skilled one on the farm, so I'd go first, and nobody else round Millbridge is hiring.
S1.do: Joins the farmworkers' union and goes to meetings in the market hall. Sells her car and cycles to work to cut costs, and writes to the council asking for publicly funded training.
S1.feel: Sick with dread, like waiting for bad news from the vet.
S1.quote: Ruth would fight for me, I think, but she'd lose that argument, because the robot doesn't need Sundays off.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Uma's fear becomes real: her job is the hands-on part robots target, and she knows she's the most replaceable person on the farm. She chooses group action and cutting back over learning the technology, and says so plainly. She wants the government, not charity, to be the safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say they've done it, they've actually done it, and nobody asked us. I'd say it should be stopped until there's a plan for people like me. I'd go to any protest going, even if it's ten people outside the council offices in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it means I'm finished in farming before I've even got good at it. I'm 27 and I'm still learning how to set the baler, and in two years a machine will do all of it better. I wouldn't have a trade, I wouldn't have savings, and I wouldn't have any idea what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at once, the phone contract, the gym I never use, eating out. I'd sign up for whatever government support there is the minute it exists, and push the union to fight for a wage that comes whether you work or not. Tomas and I would probably have to move in with his parents in their spare room in Lowford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like the floor's gone and there's nothing to grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what happens in the first month after it's clear this is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd still be milking, because the cows don't care about the news. But I'd be asking Ruth every day if they're going to keep me, and she wouldn't know either. I'd stop sleeping, I already know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about having just two years that you'd use, or is it just too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. You can't learn a trade in two years when every trade is going. Maybe I'd use it to get the union to fight for something, a payment for farmworkers, before it all lands, but I don't believe I'd win in time.

S2.say: They've actually done it, and nobody asked us. It should be stopped until there's a plan for people like me, and I'll stand outside the council offices in the rain to say so.
S2.think: I'd be finished in farming before I've even got good at it. I'd have no trade, no savings and no idea what to do next.
S2.do: Cuts her phone contract, gym and eating out at once and signs up for any government support as soon as it exists. Pushes the union for a guaranteed income, and may move with Tomas into his parents' spare room in Lowford.
S2.feel: Panicked, like the floor has gone and there's nothing to hold on to.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and I'm still learning how to set the baler, and in two years a machine will do all of it better.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Uma sees no way through: no money, no trade, no time, and she says she'd stop sleeping. She keeps working because the cows still need milking, which grounds her. Her only plan is collective: protests, the union, and government support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that we need rules before this lands, not after. But with five years I'd say it louder and to more people, because there'd be time to organise. I'd want farmworkers at the table when the plan gets written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still means my job goes, just later. Five years would take me to 32, and I'd still be the junior one, still not much better off. It's a slower version of the same ending for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get properly involved in the union, maybe help run the Millbridge branch, because nobody else my age will. I'd try to save something, even fifty a month, in a jar if I have to. I'd keep working for the Haldanes as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but less like I'm drowning. More like watching a flood come up the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means there's time for the government to do something, if people push. Two years, they'd still be arguing when it hit. So five years is the difference between fighting and just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the person who learns the robot. With five years, would you reconsider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a bit. Ruth's said before that if the robot came, someone would need to clean it, check the cows it flags as sick, deal with the alarms at 3 a.m. I'd hate it, but I'd rather do that than nothing. I'm still not sure I'd be any good.

S3.say: We need rules before this lands, not after, and with five years there's time to organise. Farmworkers should be at the table when the plan gets written.
S3.think: It's a slower version of the same ending for me. My job still goes, and at 32 I'd still be the junior one and not much better off.
S3.do: Gets involved in running the Millbridge union branch and tries to save even fifty a month. Keeps working for the Haldanes as long as they'll have her and might reluctantly learn to tend a milking robot.
S3.feel: Still frightened, but more like watching a flood rise than drowning.
S3.quote: Two years, they'd still be arguing when it hit. So five years is the difference between fighting and just reacting.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't change Uma's ending, but it changes her role: from someone things happen to, to someone organising. For the first time she half-considers learning to tend a robot, though she doubts she'd be good at it. The extra time matters most to her as time for politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse for leaving rural workers behind this time. I'd say it at the union, and I'd vote for whoever promises a real plan. I'd probably still make the joke about robots scraping the yard, because it's still funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like a lot, but I know how I am. I'd tell myself I'll sort it next year, every year. The end point is the same, I'd still be out of farm work, and I don't trust myself to get ready in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep milking and stay with the union, and try to get some savings going, a month's rent maybe. I'd push for the training to be paid for, because I won't pay for it myself. Mostly I'd wait to see what the government and the farm actually do, because ten years is a long time to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, all the way down. Not panic, but it never goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, you'd be 37 when it arrives. What does that do to your plans for your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas and I talked about kids, someday. With ten years I'd think, do we really want to bring a baby into this? I'd probably put it off, but then I was going to put it off anyway because of the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the government offered paid training in the next few years, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was paid, and near home, and I could do it in the winter when the farm's quieter, then yes, maybe. I'd want it to be something with animals still, like a vet nurse course. Something where a frightened cow still needs a person.

S4.say: We've got ten years, so there's no excuse for leaving rural workers behind this time. I'll vote for whoever has a real plan, and the robots can still come and scrape the yard at five.
S4.think: Ten years sounds like a lot, but I know I'd tell myself I'll sort it next year, every year. The end point is the same, and I don't trust myself to be ready in time.
S4.do: Keeps milking and stays active in the union while trying to save a month's rent. Pushes for paid training and would take a free winter course near home, ideally vet nursing, while waiting to see what the farm and government do.
S4.feel: A steady unease that never quite goes away, though not panic.
S4.quote: I'd want it to be something with animals still, like a vet nurse course. Something where a frightened cow still needs a person.
S4.fieldNote: Uma is honest that extra time may not help her, because she knows she'd put it off. Still, she shows the most openness here, naming vet nursing if it's free and near home. She calls it unease, but the pressure is clear enough that she is rethinking whether to have children, so I've recorded her as anxious rather than uneasy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is money that comes in whether the farm needs me or not, paid by the people making the robots, and training that's free and close to home. I don't want charity, I want my share.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the jobs, but nobody asks who decides how the animals get treated when there's no person in the shed at night. I worry about that almost as much as my wage.

headlineQuote: I don't want charity, I want my share.
portrait: Uma Petrov is 27 and the most junior hand on the Haldanes' sixty-cow dairy and barley farm near Millbridge, with about two weeks of savings and a partner who drives a parcel van. She loves the cows, avoids new technology and has never used an AI tool. She is calm about the AI Plateau but becomes alarmed as soon as robots enter the picture, because milking and scraping are exactly her hours. Her answers are always collective: join the union, push the council, demand public support. Extra warning time matters to her mainly as time to organise, and she admits she'd probably put off retraining herself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years leaves no time to learn anything new when every trade is going.
whatWouldHelp: Money that comes in whether the farm needs her or not, paid for by those who make the robots, plus free training close to home.
